# Lessons — e-fin1-finqa-skill-verifier

Experiment: replicate the coding-domain adversarial skill-verifier lift
(precision 0.40→0.92, 2.3×) on FinQA financial numeric QA. **Result: NULL.**
See `results/analysis.md` for full numbers.

---

### [meta/verification]: The adversarial-verifier lift requires a verification asymmetry, not just "adversarial framing"

<!-- captured: 2026-06-21 | stage: 7 -->

The headline finding. Confirmatory→adversarial reframing gave **0.99× lift** on
FinQA (precision 0.740 adv vs 0.745 conf; AUC 0.565 vs 0.629), versus **2.3×** in
the coding domain. Both verifiers sit at the agent's base rate (0.71) — neither
discriminates correct from incorrect answers.

**Why**: the coding-domain adversarial verifier reasons about an artifact with a
*deterministic external oracle* (the hidden test suite). The FinQA verifier has
no oracle — to "attack" an answer it must itself redo the table-lookup +
arithmetic the agent did. **Same-tier verifier (Haiku) makes the same class of
mistakes as the same-tier agent (Haiku)**, so confident adversarial recomputation
rubber-stamps the agent's errors: 19/29 wrong answers got 4/4 "likely_correct";
only 34% of true errors were flagged at all.

**The general principle**: adversarial verification lifts precision only when
*checking is easier/more reliable than generating* (a verification asymmetry).
Coding has it via test execution. Outcome-only numeric QA at a fixed model tier
does **not**. "Adversarial framing" is not itself the active ingredient — the
asymmetry is.

**Why it matters**: this is the first non-coding empirical anchor for the
verification playbook, and it is *applicability-bounding*, not confirming. The
Part-4 cross-domain projections should NOT cite FinQA as positive support; they
should be re-scoped to "domains with a verification asymmetry (test/exec oracle)."

**How to apply**: before claiming the adversarial verifier will help in a new
domain, ask "does the verifier have a cheaper/more-reliable correctness check
than re-deriving the answer?" If verifier and generator are the same tier and
share failure modes with no external oracle, expect ≈1.0× lift. See
[[verifier-reward]] for the coding baseline this fails to replicate.

---

### [meta/calibration]: Off-coding, the Claude adversarial verifier ENGAGES but does not DISCRIMINATE — abstention is not the failure mode

<!-- captured: 2026-06-21 | stage: 7 -->

RQ2 asked whether calibration drift (defaulting to "uncertain") explains a null,
as the coding-domain T4 found for non-Claude models. **For Claude on FinQA: no.**
The adversarial verifier is decisive — 318/400 calls `likely_correct`, 61
`uncertain`, 21 `likely_incorrect`; the per-example vote histogram is bimodal
(73 examples at 4/4, 15 at 0/4). It is NOT hedging.

The lesson: **engagement ≠ discrimination.** A verifier can be well-calibrated in
the "doesn't abstain" sense and still be near-random (AUC 0.57) because it is
*confidently wrong* as often as confidently right. The coding-domain framing
("only Claude calibrates") was about abstention; this shows a second, independent
axis — discriminative power — that a domain can fail on even with a calibrated
Claude verifier.

**How to apply**: when a verifier underperforms, separate two diagnoses: (a) it
abstains/defaults-to-uncertain (calibration, fixable by model choice — the T4
story), vs (b) it commits confidently but wrongly (no verification asymmetry,
NOT fixable by prompt or by switching to another same-tier model). FinQA is (b).

**Cross-verifier confirmation (n=40)**: Haiku and Nova-Pro give the *identical*
0.92× adversarial lift on the same subset (Haiku conf 0.658/adv 0.607; Nova conf
0.625/adv 0.577). Critically, Nova fails the SAME way Claude does — by confidently
affirming wrong answers (133/160 likely_correct), NOT by abstaining as it did in
the coding-domain T4. **This is the key disambiguator: the FinQA null is a
domain/asymmetry property, not a verifier-model-choice confound.** A null that
reproduces across two unrelated model families with the same engaged-but-wrong
signature is structural. Results in `results/cross_verifier_nova.jsonl`.

---

### [eval/scoring]: FinQA exe_ans has TWO ground-truth traps — percent/ratio inconsistency and free-text/multi-number answers

<!-- captured: 2026-06-21 | stage: 1 -->

`qa.exe_ans` stores percents inconsistently: "93.5%" → `0.935` (ratio form) but
"24.69%" → `24.69136` (already scaled). A correct matcher must accept gold,
gold×100, AND gold÷100. Additionally ~6% of answers are free-text/multi-number
("$22.57 billion", "0.58 or 57.5%") that a naive float parser drops.

**Fix**: `finqa_common.exact_match()` reconciles all three percent scalings and
uses 1% relative tolerance (FinQA gold is round-to-5-decimals vs human 2–3
sig-figs). The Stage-0 smoke test (`smoke_test.py`) caught a too-loose absolute
tolerance floor BEFORE the n=100 run — directly the verification-primitives
"never assume the eval harness works" lesson paying off.

**Audit your label noise**: 11/29 "wrong" answers were scoring artifacts (6
parse-fail magnitude-correct, 5 sign/representation), not agent errors — the
[[verifier-reward]] "recall ceiling is semantic-mismatch not noise" lesson
reproduced exactly. Re-scoring with the recoverable cases corrected moved base
rate 0.71→0.80 but left the adv-vs-conf lift at 1.01× — **label noise hits both
verifiers equally and cannot create or hide a differential lift.** Always re-run
the headline differential under a noise-corrected relabel to prove robustness.

### [ops/bedrock]: No boto3 needed — `aws bedrock-runtime converse` CLI is sufficient and returns token usage

<!-- captured: 2026-06-21 | stage: 1 -->

This host had aws-cli/2.x but no pip/boto3/uv. The `converse` CLI op returns
`usage.inputTokens/outputTokens` (same field names for Claude AND Amazon Nova),
which is all that's needed for cost accounting. `finqa_common.call_bedrock()`
shells out to it with tempfile message payloads + throttle backoff. Region was
us-east-2; Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6, and `us.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0` all callable.
Nova requires the `us.` inference-profile prefix (bare `amazon.nova-pro-v1:0`
errors with "on-demand throughput isn't supported"). Mistral Large not available.

**How to apply**: API-only autoresearch experiments do not need a Python SDK —
the AWS CLI converse path works for batch eval and is the fallback when pip is
absent. Throttling is real at sustained call rates; add exponential backoff.

---

### [ops/cost]: $0.03/eval ceiling holds comfortably on FinQA ($0.0134/eval) — table context did not blow the budget

<!-- captured: 2026-06-21 | stage: 7 -->

RQ3: the 4-call adversarial ensemble cost **$0.01341/eval** (45% of the $0.03
ceiling; $0.01073 under coding-domain Haiku pricing). Avg input 5,788 tok, output
1,524 tok/eval. Scoping context to `gold_inds` (the retrieval oracle) instead of
full pre_text/post_text kept inputs small. The feared table-context cost blowup
(RQ3) did not materialize. Cost was never the binding constraint — discrimination
was.
